pr_title: s_server: Do not use SSL_sendfile when KTLS is not being used
pr_body:
Fix a bug in `openssl s_server -WWW` where it would attempt to invoke `SSL_sendfile` if `-ktls -sendfile` was passed on the command line, even if KTLS has not actually been enabled, for example because it is not supported by the host. Since `SSL_sendfile` is only supported when KTLS is actually being used, this resulted in a failure to serve requests.

Fixes #17503.

Taking advice on how to test this, as most usage of `s_server` in the test suite seems to be incidental via TLSProxy rather than testing of `s_server` itself.
pr_comments: Updated to add a warning when sendfile was requested but a request was served without it.

> There is a "get out clause" in the test policy which says we don't have to write tests "where writing the test would result in disproportionately more effort than writing the code being tested"

IMO this is well within this clause. Writing a completely new test recipe that would not be trivial for this few line fix would be disproportionately more effort. However! We should at least create an issue to add tests for s_server/s_client apps.

24 hours has passed since 'approval: done' was set, but as this PR has been updated in that time the label 'approval: ready to merge' is not being automatically set.  Please review the updates and set the label manually.

comments:
I found out, what was wrong: when I did that I forgot to load the kernel module.
after I did `sudo modprobe tls` the SSL_sendfile started to work.
So I think if that kernel module is not loaded, there should be a message, and the
SSL_sendfile should not be used.

> So I think if that kernel module is not loaded,

Or basically any scenario which results in KTLS not being used. The man3 pages document that this functionality is only available if KTLS is, and describes how to test for that. We just don't do that test in s_server.
Ah, yeah, we learned that if the client uses RFC 6066 that will also make the KTLS not usable.

> Ah, yeah, we learned that if the client uses RFC 6066 that will also make the KTLS not usable.

Can also happen if KTLS doesn't support the ciphersuite, or if compression is negotiated.

> Ah, yeah, we learned that if the client uses RFC 6066 that will also make the KTLS not usable.

This point was already clarified on #17504 , but for the archives: RFC 6066 is the (current) generic "extensions for TLS"  RFC, that documents a large handful of different extensions.  The relevant one here is "max_fragment_length".

To rectify this I'm looking for a canonical function to determine if KTLS is enabled on a connection.

SSL_sendfile uses `BIO_get_ktls_send(s->wbio)`, which requires access to `s->wbio`. However, `SSL_get_wbio` may return `s->bbio` instead of `s->wbio`, and I'm uncertain whether this is an issue (anyone care to confirm?)

Possibly worth also pointing out that bio_ssl doesn't implement `BIO_CTRL_GET_KTLS_{SEND,RECV}`, so `BIO_get_ktls_{send,recv}` won't work on SSL BIOs. Is this intended behaviour?

Broadly speaking:

  * If there is a canonical way to test whether KTLS is enabled on a SSL object, let me know.
    If there isn't, we should probably have one as otherwise it's hard for a consumer of the API to tell if `SSL_sendfile` will work.
  * Maybe consider implementing `BIO_CTRL_GET_KTLS_{SEND,RECV}` via the above API.

> SSL_sendfile uses BIO_get_ktls_send(s->wbio), which requires access to s->wbio. However, SSL_get_wbio may return s->bbio instead of s->wbio, and I'm uncertain whether this is an issue (anyone care to confirm?)

The `SSL_sendfile` documentation recommends using `BIO_get_ktls_send()` for this purpose:
https://www.openssl.org/docs/man3.0/man3/SSL_sendfile.html

In actual fact if a bbio is present then `SSL_get_wbio()` will still not return it, but will return the true underlying wbio:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d2d2401aed7ff45f4c013201944e1218dce12da7/ssl/ssl_lib.c#L1335-L1345

Although in actual fact it wouldn't really matter in practice because a buffer bio is a filter bio. `BIO_get_ktls_send()` is really just a call to `BIO_ctrl`. Filter BIOs typically just pass any ctrl commands they don't understand to the underlying BIO. In the buffer BIO case:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d2d2401aed7ff45f4c013201944e1218dce12da7/crypto/bio/bf_buff.c#L401-L405
